utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. There is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse from the fact that the witness has already been brought in I take it there are no procedural issues at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: None that I need to raise with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I may take it that you're ready to call Mr. Maricic as your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, before you start giving evidence in this Court, let me first ask you whether you hear me in a language you understand. Yes. And let me say "Dobro jutro" to you as well. Mr. Maricic before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require to you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maricic. Please be seated. Mr. Josse, looking at the 65 ter summary, I wondered to what extent leave it at this moment to you, to what extent some of the evidence was repetitious. I mean power-sharing agreements, et cetera, et cetera. We heard that very often and I never understood this to be disputed by the Prosecution. Of course, if there are certain details --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I honestly think Your Honour can rest assured that I'm aware of that. Your Honour, perhaps when the witness is out of court, I am more than willing to tell the Court the process of the production of the 65 ters. What's contained within the 65 ter has far more to do with what material is available at the time we prepare them rather than necessarily what we actually want to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I say, I'm more than happy to examine that process at another juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. Sometimes it's perhaps a bit of a gamble. Sometimes what is in 65 ter is not the subject of the examination and sometimes I hear complaints about matters raised during the examination but do not appear in the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. We've been quite frank about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's get started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, your name is Bosko Maricic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Bosko Maricic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You'll have to excuse my pronunciation on occasions, Mr. Maricic. It's very poor but feel free to correct me if it's apparent that I'm mispronouncing something. You're from the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were educated there and --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as relevance to this case is concerned, sometime prior to the war, you became a restaurateur in a place called Brka in the municipality of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll look at the geography in a few moments' time. Just tell the Chamber when you first owned that restaurant in Brka?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You sold that restaurant in 1991 and went to live in Brcko town itself?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were vice-president of the local SDS?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You had been in the League of Communists up until --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You stood unsuccessfully in the 1990 multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were mobilised very soon after the war began, at the beginning of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And on the 16th of May you were badly injured, wounded, in fact, and then spent many months in Serbia. Again we'll turn to that in more detail in due course.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You returned in September of 1992 to the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And after the war, you became the director of a local furniture factory and continued to be involved in municipal affairs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a very brief overview, Mr. Maricic. Let's go back and examine your restaurant in Brka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my learned friend's case manager, Your Honour. He's provided a number of copies of the Brcko coloured map. Perhaps one could go on the ELMO. I don't know whether this needs a specific number. It's, of course, part of a -- batch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there will be no marking, I don't think it needs a separate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, this is part of 527, Prosecution Exhibit 527.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you point to Brka, please, Mr. Maricic, on the map that is on the ELMO, which is the machine to the right of you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: [Witness points]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, there are two Brkas on this map, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And on the map they're both described with exactly the same name, Brka, B-r-k-a, why is that, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: This Brka that I showed is populated exclusively by Muslims, whereas the other Brka more to the right is called Serb Brka, although it's not officially the title, it's not written on the map, but it's populated solely by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Which of these two places was your restaurant situated in?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: In the Muslim Brka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very approximately, what was the proportion of Serbs to Muslims in that place?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: In Brka? I was the only Serb in the Brka where I had my eatery.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about your customers? What ethnicity were they in general?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: They were 90 per cent Muslims, local Muslims, and people from the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber what the population of Muslim Brka was? I'll call it that for ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly but around 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did the ethnic tensions, which as the learned Judge has already observed this Court is well aware of, affect your business at all?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you tell the Chamber how it affected your business?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Brka village, which is exclusively populated by Muslims is halfway to Bukvik village where I was born. I used that road very often to travel to my home village, but in Brka, since I used to play football, there were other football players with whom I was friends, very good friends. I continued to have friends in that Brka and that's one of the reasons why I bought land there and opened a catering establishment and moved there to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you just show the Chamber again, using the machine to your right, where Bukvik village is?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to change my glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see you pointed to something which, as I read, it says Bukvik Gornji. Is that the place you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: No. I showed Donji Bukvik, and there is another, Gornji Bukvik right above that. I was born in Donji Bukvik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. We can see the area. Thank you. And you've told the Chamber that you bought this business in Brka, and you were explaining how things started to go wrong. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I bought a parcel of land, built a house. I opened a complex establishment, including a catering establishment, but not only that, and moved there to live with my wife and child. I had a rather successful business. However, as years passed, interethnic tensions rose in the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina including the area of Brcko, and one day I woke up to the fact that I was a Serb and people held a grudge against me because I was a Serb, and had a successful business in a Muslim place. There were other catering establishments owned by some Muslims and one Croat woman who were less successful but I was a Serb, a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, and never made any bones about it. I publicly stated that I was a member of that party and that's when problems began.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how, Mr. Maricic, did these problems manifest themselves?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, but I still remember the hardest things. First of all, my Muslim friends started saying hello to me in an icy way. Then guests pretending to be drunk started to break things in my establishment. I had a TV aerial on my building, which was cut every night. On another occasion, somebody broke the windows and the glass on my entrance door, and all the leading positions in the police force in Brcko were Muslims and Croats -- were occupied by Muslims and Croats. They charged a man but did nothing about it later. This man continued to vandalise other places and bragged that he had vandalised mine. It was perhaps in January or maybe the end of 1991, one local Muslim, a thug, came into my establishment, Mehmed Vidinovic [phoen]. He asked me if I had any family. I said I had a wife and two children and he said that both his children and mine would be orphans because he was going to kill me. I told him that killing each other made no sense and let's have a drink instead together. He left. And afterwards, he bragged that during the war, he had killed a lot of my relatives. It's not just that. In my house, I had an apartment where I spent nights and I had wooden blinds on my windows, and they regularly threw stones at those blinds, shrieked and screamed all around me, so I decided I couldn't live there any more. One day, because I have to say the authorities in Brka were also replaced by some extremists and they decided that the young people from the area were no longer allowed to frequent my establishment, and they charged some people to enforce it. One day, a man approached two or three guests in my establishment and asked them what they were doing there. I'm just giving you a few examples that I can recall at the moment but there were lots of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So how did you resolve the problem?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: My establishment was a new one, had a new, good building. It was perhaps the nicest building in the centre of town, and I had a lot of prospective buyers. Mostly people originally from the village who worked abroad and who wanted me to sell it to them. I had offers of about 150.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "1150.000"] Deutschmark, maybe more. I didn't feel like selling it. However, when the situation became as I described it, I changed my mind and wanted to sell but the prospective buyers suddenly vanished. In the village, there was a married couple, Muslims, who had a business in the village and who had said once that they were willing to buy my establishment. And I went to see them. However, they were aware of the situation as well, and they wanted me to sell the place now for peanuts and I had to agree. After that, I moved to Brcko to live. At the same time in my home village, Bukvik, in a very busy place downtown, I opened an office building, not an office building but a building that can be used for businesses, intending to open a new business, a new eatery, but that idea never came through either because of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So can you give the Chamber as exact a date as possible that you sold your business in Brka and moved to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that because it was a long time ago and we were all victims of a psychosis. It no longer matters to me anyway. I think it was in the end of 1991, around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I see on the transcript what in my memory was 150.000 Deutschmarks appears as 1150.000. So that should be corrected. And perhaps could you tell us, Mr. Maricic, what finally was the price you got for your eatery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 47.000 Deutschmark was the price I sold it for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And about the date, you said it doesn't matter that much for you any more, but it may matter for the Chamber. Was it before Orthodox Christmas, was it after Orthodox Christmas? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Orthodox Christmas is in January. That would have made it already 1992. I think I sold my establishment earlier, but please don't ask me to be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But I'm just trying to give you some assistance in finding out whether it was late 1991 or early 1992. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's, if we may, Mr. Maricic, put this into some sort of perspective in terms of your political involvement. You've already told the Chamber that you stood in the 1990 elections. You stood for the BiH assembly. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As is apparent from what you've already said, you were a candidate on behalf of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were not elected but, in fact, perhaps we should have dealt with this earlier, you became a deputy in the assembly of the Serbian people or the Republika Srpska as it was by then in 1994?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that was because in effect you were a reserve, the person who was elected above you, so to speak, on the SDS list was someone called Dr. Beli and he died and you replaced him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Dr. Beli is an individual we may here a little bit about during the course of your evidence. What was his real name, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Milenko Vojinovic, and his nickname was Beli. He was also known as Beli.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you explained that the reason for that was to do with his pale appearance and he was called doctor because he was a physician; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the point that you moved to Brcko, you were vice-president of the Brcko SDS, what did that involve? What type of political commitment did that involve on your part?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Since Dr. Beli was a very strong person, he had a strong personality, I had to be a, so to say, go-for. I had to do everything. I was in charge of operations. He held all the strings in his hands and it was very rarely that I was able to stand in for him. That was only very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because he was also president of the local SDS, as well as being a deputy?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you moved to Brcko, what did you do in terms of your livelihood, a job, that type of thing?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I had some savings. I got some money that I invested into the facility that I was building, and the balance I spent on my day-to-day living.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about your political involvement when you arrived in Brcko? Did that grow? Did you do more for the party?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: A little bit more because I had more time on my hands, but not that much. I was very active.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very active in what sense?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: In the work of the party, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how did that activity manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Beli was a deputy, and I believe that he still worked as a physician in the hospital, and very often he would send me to go to this or that village to talk to the president of the local board there. He would ask me to go and do this or that. I loved to travel. I had a car. I had some money. So whenever he asked me to do something, I would gladly go, I would gladly travel around.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to ask you about the type of ethnic tensions you encountered in Brcko itself when you moved there.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: When I moved to Brcko, the ethnic tensions had already increased. In Brcko, Croats and Muslims formed a majority, and Brcko borders on Croatia in the north and, in the south, it borders on Tuzla which is also a town with a majority Muslim and Croat population. I believe that both Muslims and Croats deemed that Brcko belonged to them because they formed a majority and, of course, they were very active there, especially members of the SDA were active. The SDA being a Muslim party and also the HDZ was very active. Tensions grew and the Serbs in Brcko felt more and more intimidated and more and more threatened by the day. There were a lot of examples of pressure being put on Serbs and Serbs being intimidated. I believe that you already know that the Muslims established their party, the SDA, before the SDS was formed and Croats also formed the HDZ before the SDS was formed. A lot more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. The Chamber is aware of that, and that's, I think, exactly the type of thing that the learned Presiding Judge was alluding to earlier so far as material that we don't need to go over again is concerned. Could you give specific examples of what you say were provocations in 1991, early 1992, by Muslims against Serbs in Brcko town?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I can. If you'll allow me I would like to finish my previous thought and share a few words with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, go ahead. I'm looking at the learned -- the learned Judge says go ahead as well.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I believe - I believe - that the SDS would not have been established if the two ethnically based parties that directly threatened the Serb people had not been established first. I apologise. Can you now repeat your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. My question is: Could you give specific examples of what you say were provocations in 1991 and early 1992 by Muslims against the Serbs in the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I've already said that there were -- there were daily provocations. For example, since the managements and leaderships of all organisations consisted of all of Muslims and Croats only, in the police building, they placed a long desk, and they put up for sale videotapes and other things that are used in Islamic countries, and they played very loud ethnic, religious, Islamic music through very strong loudspeakers and we know very well over there that those are called valahi [phoen] and kasida [phoen]. Those lads that sold those things had red caps on their heads as a symbol of Islam and they were very aggressive to all of us who were Serbs and also members of the SDS. At that time, it was very difficult to be a Serb in Brcko. That is just one example. In one building, in the part of the town called Srpska Varos, with a majority Serb population, the Muslim Youth Association had been established by the SDA. That was a -- one part of the SDA party for the young. They opened an office in that part of the building and they also installed very strong loudspeakers and they played very loud Islam music until late in the night. One day, in the evening, at the beginning of 1992, I entered the Galeb hotel in Brcko. It was between 10 and 11.00 in the evening. In one part of the hotel, at a long table, ten Muslims were seated. As I was passing by, one of them whose nickname was "Car" told me, Bosko, why don't you treat us to a drink? Since I knew him, I told him, Car, I have paid enough. I stayed on. I expected a comment, and I did hear the comment although I turned my back on them, and I heard Car mentioning my mother and swearing, and then he said, "We will take him to the bridge and put a bullet through his head." Let me explain. During the Second World War, the Muslim and Croat extremists, together with the Germans almost completely destroyed the Jewish and Serb body in Brcko. There were a lot of execution sites. One of them being the bridge. They would take people to the bridge and they would kill them on that bridge and throw their bodies into the river. They killed them by hitting them with a hammer and that's what he was hinting when he commented on my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've asked you to pause simply so that you could tell the Chamber the real name of Car if you know it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: No. He was a well-known thug in Brcko. I don't know what his name was but everybody knew him by his nickname, Car.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. After he had said that to you, how did you react and what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I left. And that was over for me. And I can share another interesting case with you, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I still had a bar in Brka in 1991, and one evening, around midnight, I went to a pub called Westphalia in the suburb of Brcko. It was owned by a Muslim. I knew the people then but I can't remember their names. I entered the pub. There was a band playing. There were a lot of people. I was standing at a bar close to an aquarium with fish. I took my drink and close to me, at a table, some people were sitting, mostly Muslims. One of them stood up. His name is Hame. I believe that his family name is Slomic but I'm not sure. He was also a well known person in Brcko. He came up to me and he whispered into my here and I'll try to quote him. He said -- first he used an "F" word. And he said, "We 'F' you for 500 years and we will continue for the next 500 years." I don't know whether you have understood what I was trying to say. I complained to the owner, who was also a Muslim. The owner asked him to go back to his table, which he did, but returned to me after a few minutes and then I left the pub. These are just two examples of the things that were happening constantly and I just shared with you what happened to me but I was not an only Serb in Brcko. There were a lot of Serbs who experienced similar things and, as a result of that, people were getting more and more scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I only want to ask you about one other specific example. Did you have an encounter with a Dr. Ramic at a political meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the name, what was the full name of Dr. Ramic, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim Ramic, also known as Ibro. We called him Ibro but I believe that his full name was Ibrahim. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one other thing for clarification. Was he related in any way to someone called Mustafa Ramic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: They were brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Go on, please. Tell us about your encounter with Ibrahim Ramic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: This was an occasion when I stood in for Dr. Beli who was away on business. He called me and asked me to head an SDS delegation at negotiations between the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA. I don't know when this took place. I don't know whether it was the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992. The pressure on the Serb people had come to a head, and the assembly of Brcko at the time was a multi-ethnic assembly but the Muslims and the Croats had a majority and they made all the decisions, although the SDS had partnership relations with the SDA and the HDZ and they were supposed to participate in power sharing. However, the Muslims and the Croats were more numerous and they outvoted the Serb representatives, and one of their decisions was to review the employment policy in Brcko and then they made a decision that all Serbs should be sacked regardless of their skill or experience. They started firing everybody from company guards to management. And this was the topic of our conversation when I stood in for Dr. Beli. I told them that this was not fair, and Ibro Ramic who was Mustafa's brother but unlike Mustafa he was very edgy. Although he was a physician by profession, he reacted very stormily and he told me that it was not my place to talk. I said something else and then he stood up very angrily and said, "According to the last census there are 46 of us in Brcko. At the next census, God willing, we will be 51 per cent and you will no longer be able to live here." I reacted to that but this is an episode that had -- has direct connection with the Islamic Declaration of Alija Izetbegovic because it says there that wherever Muslims held a majority of over 51 per cent, they could create their state there and they could create their own laws. Ibrahim Ramic was a proven Islamist and I believe that he was familiar with the Islamic Declaration, and that's why he said that. But I also believe that this is exactly what he was thinking at the time, and this is the episode that happened during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned in the course of that last answer that it was decided that all Serbs should be sacked regardless of their skill or experience. Was that put into effect, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I apologise and I would like to correct you. Not all Serbs, but there was a large-scale firing of Serbs under the pretext that there was a surplus of manpower, and that's when Serbs were being fired on a large scale. Since they had already taken over the police and their people were in all the leading positions, and at that time although still there was -- there were authorities on paper, but in practice, there was nobody to complain to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you give us some specific examples of how you say Serbs were discriminated against in terms of employment? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, and this happened on such a large scale that I did not take stock of all the people, but I remember from conversations that the Serbs were being fired on a large scale and that Muslims and Catholics were brought to work instead of them. Even though they were less skillful. Sometimes they were semi-literate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me ask you specifically, then, about the police force. Were there signs of discrimination in the police force, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I will tell you what I personally experienced, and there were complaints coming from all sides. Since my restaurant was in Brka, my restaurant was often thrashed and I would report that to the police. However, I did not enjoy any protection. When my restaurant was thrashed once, the police discovered who the perpetrators there, they asked me to raise a civil suit but nobody did anything although the perpetrator was known. He was a local Muslim. As I was walking through the corridors of the police building I could see that Muslims and Croats occupied all the leading and managerial positions. There were no Serbs in any of those positions. In such a situation I could not expect any protection from the institution that was led by extreme Muslims and Croats. And this is just one example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, we are shifting from discrimination in appointments, people being fired, to discriminatory functioning of bodies which is not the same. Could you give us one example of someone who was fired because of being a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, nobody asked me that. I really cannot come up with any names. I can't give you any names, unfortunately. I really can't give you any -- any names, but it shouldn't be difficult to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you say that on a large scale, Serbs were fired and replaced by less competent others, you must know of one example in the hospital, in one of the companies, or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you mentioned the hospital, I believe that I remember that the chief administrator of the hospital was fired and that Ibro Ramic was employed in his stead. But I can't be sure of that. I just told you what I know personally. It was a long time ago and it's very difficult for me to remember any names. At that time I knew a lot of people. Some people even came directly to me to complain. I remember a guy from the municipal building. He was from Grbovica. He came to me in tears. He said I have a wife and children but I'm being fired. However, I couldn't help him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of this chief administrator of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that Dr. Ibrahim Ramic was appointed, the president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I was asking for the name of the one who was fired.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, no. I never registered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of the questions asked by the learned presiding Judge, can you assist at all with specific examples from the SUP, of discrimination against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that blatant case of discrimination is the facts that out of the seven managerial positions in the SUP, in the police, none of them were occupied by a Serb. The chief of SUP was Safet Suljagic. The head of the crime police was a Muslim, and the head of the state security was his -- one of the well known brothers in Brcko. The commander of the police, again, was Zlatko Jasarevic, a Muslim; the commander of the traffic police was another Muslim. The head of the crime police was a Muslim. In any case, the -- all the seven managerial positions in the MUP were occupied by Muslims and Croats. There were no Serbs. And since I had a lot of hardships with my restaurant, I sent a letter to the chief of police, Safet Suljagic, asking for an explanation as to why I was not being protected by the police. And then I asked him how come that he allowed for all the managerial positions to be taken over by Muslims and Croats, and not a single Serb, and I implied his communist past and his honesty. He never replied to me. He -- this Safet Suljagic spent the entire time of war in Brcko and I used to see him in the Serbian part of Brcko throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one clarification? This Muslims and Croats exclusively in managerial positions, was that since the multi-party elections or was this the result of any Serbs having been in such positions being fired? So I want you -- I would like to know whether this was -- well, let's say, what one might consider as an abuse of power on from the beginning or whether this was the result of an earlier sharing of power and then subsequently firing of Serbs who had such positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That situation, where all the high-ranking people in the police were Muslims and Croats. No Serbs prevailed before the multi-party elections and before the power-sharing agreement among the three parties. So in my judgement it was done deliberately in anticipation of future events. When the partnership agreement between the three parties was made and I don't remember when that was, there were still a couple of examples at the very outset when Serbs did get a few positions. Such an example was the president of municipality, who was a Serb, and Pero Markovic occupied another leading position. But they had to abide by this agreement only before the war. Afterwards, the gloves were off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the power sharing --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just for a moment? Did you just mention the name Mustafa Ramic in the answer you gave?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It doesn't come out in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't. Could you tell us in what context you mentioned Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Mustafa Ramic became president of the municipal assembly of Brcko through partnership negotiations. He was brother of Ibrahim Ramic who was president of the SDA. Mustafa was more moderate person than his brother Ibrahim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I did understand you well that under the power-sharing agreement, that all managerial police functions had been and remained in the hands of Muslims and Croats; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. After these partnership talks, I cannot really remember, but it is a possibility that this structure was improved a little but only at the very top. Thus in the municipal assembly, the president was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm exclusively at this moment asking you about the police force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that before the partnership talks, all the leading positions were occupied by Muslims and Croats. I can only assume that it was from 1987 until 1990. That's my assumption. But after the partnership talks after the elections, it's possible, although I can't recall precisely, that the Serbs were represented by a few persons, but most certainly only at a very low level because a Croat became head of the SUP, head of the investigations became a Muslim, another Jasarevic occupied another leading position in the police. So that these partnership talks brought only very small improvements in the police and in the municipality, whereas lower down, on lower levels, a purge was effected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the highest-level Serb in the police force after the partnership talks? Who was it and what was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember one man who had come to Brcko, a Serb. He was a native from Brcko and he said that he was a commander somewhere in Croatia, Split or Zadar, and he said that in Croatia, Serbs could not survive in senior positions because the interethnic tensions had brought about massive dismissals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he the highest Serb, highest-level Serb in the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he was a commander of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse. For the Chamber, it's important to have a clear view on such matters. It was not very clear and the time also, what changed, when it changed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you clarify this, please, Mr. Maricic? Earlier, when you mentioned Mustafa Ramic and his name did not come out in the translation, you said, didn't you, that Pero Markovic was the leading Serb and he was president of the executive committee?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I don't think he was the leading Serb. I don't know what you understand that to mean. If you mean positions in the municipal authorities, then he was, but he was a Serb deputy occupying the position of the president of the executive council, which means municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We were simply trying to sort out here the answer that you had previously given but that clarifies it. Are you able to name any Serbs in the SUP, whom you say were dismissed because they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I can't. I don't remember any names. It was a long time ago. It got all mixed up in my head. And I'm not very good at remembering names. That's the best I can tell you. They were dismissed gradually already before the multi-party elections there were no Serbs in senior positions. And later on, they continued to be dismissed, phased out. I cannot describe that entire period in terms of names. I just happen to remember the names of the leading Croats and Muslims in top positions in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like now to move on to a completely different topic, and that is the arming of the various ethnic groups within the municipality in the lead-up to the war. I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, but there is a general allegation, certainly as far as Brcko is concerned, that Serbs were being armed by the JNA in the lead-up to the war in the spring of 1992. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: The JNA was made up of all ethnicities. However, in the lead-up to the crisis, the JNA was abandoned by both Muslims and Croats, and mainly Serbs remained in it. Since the SDS, where I was vice-president, was anticommunist and rightist, it was on bad terms with communists and all the leading people in the JNA were communists, so that they had their reservations in relation to the SDS, and even made some problems for the SDS. However, when the war began, or, rather, just prior to that, it was well known that Muslims and Croats were getting armed and some explosions had already happened around Vukovar, and the Serb people were living in a psychosis of fear, in panic. It was already the beginning of 1992. There was no longer any talk of who belonged to which party except perhaps for the communists. The SDS and all the other parties of democratic orientation gathered to discuss what needs to be done to save the people, because the memories from the Second World War were fresh. Brcko had a large body of Serb intellectuals. Let me just remember, a lawyer, Rizda Zelenovic [phoen], Dr. Beli, and many other professors and Ph.D.s, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You take a lot of time to tell us a lot of details but could you perhaps start with answering the question? It might be that at the very end, that you come to an answer, but we would like to you answer the question, if we would like to know more details then we -- the question was: What you say about a general allegation, certainly as far as Brcko is concerned, that Serbs were being armed by the JNA. Did this take place? Yes or no? And then perhaps reasons why or -- could be further explored, but did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a certain quantity of arms that Serbs did receive from the JNA just before the war. Not much. Not enough. But they did get something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Josse, if you would like to, of course, if you would like to know further details but I would like to focus the witness, first of all, answering the question and then come with the details and the whys and the whens, et cetera. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How and when did you become aware of what you just stated?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Well, I was privy to a lot of things that were happening in Brcko, and it couldn't pass me by, something like this. I was vice-president of the party and I was concerned over the matter, and I was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In what way were you informed? What was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Well, I know because my home village of Bukvik was already encircled, people were in great danger, and around 50 rifles had been taken there in one consignment, the old-fashioned kind of rifle. I visited my family in Bukvik when I heard from people that they had received those rifles from the JNA. Of course, very few and very bad quality. If you allow me to say the JNA was a communists and they primarily armed what they called proletarians so they distributed the automatic rifles they had to the proletarians, and for the rest of the people, they had only the M-41s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you mean by the word proletarians in this context?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Well, communists, and the term proletarian dates back to the Second World War. They were fighters called proletarians, or maybe communist politicians. You know the slogan invented by Lenin, I believe, proletarians of all countries unite.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the time or subsequently, did you become aware or have you become aware of the supply of arms to Serbs, again in 1991-1992, from sources other than the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question already. I said that I had visited my home village of Bukvik and some villagers told me that they had received rifles. I believe in 1991 there was very little arms' supply, but just before the war and before the escalation of combat, it did happen, not only in my home village of Bukvik but in other Serb villages too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May have been my misunderstanding, Mr. Maricic, but this supply that you have just mentioned came from where? What was the source of the supply?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. I don't know, what purchases -- what supply do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've asked you initially about the supply of arms from the JNA. You've answered that. I'm now asking you to focus your attention, if you're able to help, on arms that were supplied from sources other than the JNA.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you help with that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you can hear me. I think something is not switched on. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can hear you, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, then. In this general panic, Serbs were looking for a way out, for a way to save themselves, to defend themselves. This rifle was priceless because everybody knows you can defend yourself only with a rifle. And I remember that it was a Serb living in Vienna who purchased perhaps around 40 trophy rifles, the M-41, and brought them to Brcko. I personally bought myself a rifle for 1600 Deutschmark from a man who lived in Switzerland. It was the shotgun kind. And I know that everybody was looking to buy a gun, just to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This supply of 40 trophy rifles from Vienna, how did you learn about that? We don't need detail, just an idea.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Well, I had friends everywhere, including Brcko, and one of these friends used to livable in Vienna and was friends with that man, whose name is Luka Pekic. He had an establishment in Vienna and he was standing with this Luka person outside the Galeb hotel and this friend told me that Luka had provided 50 rifles, that he would pay for in Vienna. Those were trophy rifles, and as I understood he bought them for 2 or 3 Deutschmarks each. And those rifles were indeed brought -- I saw them, they were really museum pieces. I even heard the details of how they were shipped in the back of a passenger car, driven by a Hungarian. Then this man went to collect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst it might be obvious, the Chamber might so consider your answer that you bought a gun to defend yourself as important. And perhaps you could explain your motives in a little bit more detail.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I'm a man of the people, close to the people, and what the people were feeling I felt myself. The people were feeling in great danger. I'm also well-read, and I read a lot about history and geography. I knew a lot about our history and it was clear to me that we were in for a great tragedy unless we find a way to save ourselves. I am not a huntsman but still I bought that hunting rifle for self-defence, if something happens. That was my motive. Generally speaking, people in Brcko were very afraid by that time already. They had sent their wives and children to Serbia to safety and it was mainly able-bodied men who stayed lined to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, have you dealt with the JNA arming? Because I would like to know a few more details on arms coming from the JNA. Mr. Maricic, you told us that the JNA was communist and that they primarily armed what they called proletarians. I'm trying to understand how this happened. How would they know who would be a proletarian, to deliver a weapon to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I'm concerned, that's very clear. In the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia, the Communist Party had all the power and all the officers were communists. Before the war, and generally speaking the army had its intelligence service, they knew everything about everybody. They knew how people breathed, let alone to which party they belonged. They were completely informed about everything. It was not just the JNA in Bosnia and Yugoslavia. There were a lot of semi-military organisations, the civilian defence, the TO, and all these people in all these military agencies had to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also told us that the JNA was, the Croats and the Muslims had left the JNA. So what remained in the JNA was mainly Serbs then, is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how did they distribute those weapons? Would they go from door to door to proletarians or how was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The arming of proletarians was held a big secret. It had been done a bit earlier and I found about it from my own villagers who told me about volleys of automatic fire in the night. But what they brought to the regular people, they brought to the village, they had their own men there, representatives who distributed, and they distributed to regular people the lower quality weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you -- could you be a bit more specific? You said they had their own men there. Could you tell us, for example, in the village where you came from, who would receive the weapons and further distribute them? Let's concentrate on Bukvik because I do understand that that's what you consider your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The list of proletarians, quote unquote, who received the weapons, through some channels reached the Muslim side in the war and they read it over the radio, including the number of weapons these people had received, including for Bukvik. I cannot give you the details about Bukvik because I no longer lived there at the time. I just visited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who had that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That list was read over the radio by the Muslims. It was read on the Muslim radio once they took over the area of Bukvik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm totally confused now because your earlier answers were about -- but let me check that. Mr. Josse, please correct me when I'm wrong. The question was about Serbs being armed by the JNA. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was the basis of the question certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now you're talking about Muslims. But we were talking about Serbs being armed by the JNA. So I do not understand how Muslims started reading the lists of the proletarians who received those arms, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll let the witness deal with it but that is logical, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us how this -- or was it once they had taken over the area that they read that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, before Bukvik was taken over, I mean, you said you were told how this distribution of arms happened. Who received them? Or did they go door by door and deliver individual rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the war had practically already started, everybody knew there would be a war, and I've already told you that the JNA was represented somehow in every village and there was also the Territorial Defence and the civilian defence. Those lists of TO and civilian defence were activated. They included able-bodied men and there were even some women in the civilian defence, although I don't believe that they were armed, and I think the distribution of weapons was done according to those lists, village by village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier said that weapons were distributed to proletarians. Now you are, at least from what I understand, suggesting that it was TO members and civilian defence that were given arms. Were they all proletarians or how should I understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not all proletarians in the civilian protection and the Territorial Defence. All the able-bodied civilians were members of the TO and the CZ, and proletarians were a secret organisation, and I believe that most of these proletarians were associates of the military secret services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same time you said so, apart from proletarians being armed the TO members and civilians were -- civilian defence members were also armed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But we are talking small quantities. For example, a village of 150 or 200 villagers were given maybe 15 rifles. That's what I heard. That's what I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And were these arms, that was no secret, that they were distributed, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not exactly in the open. It was semi-secret, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now, semi-secret. Who was involved in this semi-secret distribution of arms? So I do understand proletarians was fully secret, then we have the semi-secret distribution of arms to TO members and civilian defence members. Who organised this? I mean, who -- if you have 15 arms -- 15 rifles on a population of 150 or 200, who would say, you get a rifle, you get a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly but I suppose that the TO had its management and that the -- those who were in charge of the TO had the main say in the distribution of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And civilian defence as well? Or is there -- you used the two terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The civilian defence is a very broad term, and I believe that once it was dismantled, and this was happening slowly, all that remained was the TO, and the communists held the entire population under -- under their control. They formed this civilian protection to involve everybody, even the elderly women in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were these arms distributed in Serb villages only or -- I mean, was the JNA, because that was the start of the questions, was the JNA arming Serbs or would they arm Muslim villages as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the Serb villages. I don't know about the Muslim villages. Since they had abandoned the JNA, and that at the time the JNA in Brcko was reduced to some 20 people, only officers there. I wouldn't know anything about the Muslim villages, although I'm aware of the information that in the Muslim village called Brezevo Polje, the TO had been established on the eve of the war, that it consisted of 90 per cent Muslims and that they were also given weapons and they even participated in fighting at the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in the Serb villages, TO management was in whose hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was semi-military structure and, of course, that the JNA had the main say in the appointment of commanders because in that structure, the command staff had to be theirs, exclusively theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now in your village, let's concentrate on Bukvik. Who was in command of the TO in Bukvik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know. It was a semi-secret for me. I was against communists, and no such information was available to me, and I suppose I wasn't really interested in all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the TO was not a communist or a specifically communist organisation, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it or was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. It wasn't. It wasn't. It was a mass organisation. There were people in it who were not communists but the leading -- the commanding staff were all communists, close to the JNA, and nothing could happen without their knowledge. Let me just say that the TO commander would always hold a very high military rank in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as far as TO command is concerned, you were a member of the SDS. Was -- were SDS members in the municipality, not specifically in Bukvik, from what you said you wouldn't know, but were SDS members in command positions in the TO in the municipality of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They were anticommunists. The SDS was mainly an anticommunist, right-wing organisation, and none of them could ever be appointed to any of those positions. I'm not talking about the beginning of the war. At that time it was all already All People's Defence but that was not the case before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But your last answer is not entirely clear to me. Are you saying that SDS members would be in command positions at the beginning of the war but not before? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the war started, then some members of the SDS who had some military knowledge were appointed to command positions but this was no longer known as the Territorial Defence but rather as All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do therefore understand that even in Serb villages, SDS members -- well, let's say prior to the war, let's say prior to what -- should I say, April 1992, were not in command positions in the TO. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's a correct understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for these clarifications. Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock. At the same time, I -- well, I thought you had dealt with the arming through the JNA, only intervened at a stage where I thought you had finished with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to move on after the break to what the witness knows about the arming of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then I'll deal with the arming of Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I have received an urgent request from one of the other Trial Chambers, who has difficulties in finalising a videolink. The request would be that we would sit tomorrow instead of during the morning, in the afternoon, in Courtroom I instead of in the morning in Courtroom II. Is there any -- I'm not asking whether there is any objection. I'm asking whether there is any insurmountable problem involved in that. I can tell you that the Judges had to reschedule their own programmes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have a minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am getting Mr. Karganovic to check but the next witness is arriving tomorrow. I'm due to call him. I am unclear when he's arriving. If he's arriving -- we'll know in a minute. Mr. Karganovic is checking. If he's arriving in the morning as I had thought, then I had planned to see him tomorrow afternoon, take him to the prison on Thursday morning and call him on Thursday afternoon. Therefore, if we are sitting tomorrow afternoon, it would make a significant amount of difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. On the other hand, you may be aware, Mr. Josse, that the Trial Chamber always tries to accommodate as best as it can and sometimes even would not make any changes in the programme but here there is an important videolink involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I can do is tell the Court. If this be the position, just how difficult -- basically, I won't have enough time to proof the next witness if I'm right about his time of arrival. It's as plain and simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see whether there are any other possible solutions as well. But one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He is due here at lunchtime tomorrow. So what was going through my mind is correct. The only thing I would say, in fairness, putting all cards on the table, of course, there is a possibility that Mr. Maricic will still be in the witness box on Thursday and therefore I won't need to call Mr. Krsman until Friday. But, Your Honour, if I'm going to call Mr. Krsman at all on Thursday, then realistically I need to spend some of tomorrow afternoon with him so it would make a significant difference to our preparations. That's all I can fairly say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, having listened to you, I instructed the Chamber staff to see whether there are any alternative solutions. If not, the Chamber might decide that we would nevertheless sit tomorrow in the afternoon. Please proceed. Mr. Maricic, this was a procedural issue. You're not involved in it in any way but Mr. Josse will now continue to examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I indicated, Mr. Maricic, before the break, I next want to ask you about your state of knowledge so far as the arming of Muslims are concerned prior to the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I don't have detailed information on that. After the war, I learned that they had done that before. At the time the Muslims and the Croats had been armed through their Patriotic Leagues and some other semi-military organisations, even before their parties were established, and all that had installed panic into the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The source of the information, vague as it may be, that you have just told the Chamber about?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: After the war, in Brcko, some Muslims bragged that they had transported the weapons across the Sava from Croatia and armed their people. They spoke about that publicly. They never hid the fact. We had information, but no source of it. I personally believe that the military intelligence service was aware of all that, and all that reached us was some information without any precise details. But all this was aimed at creating panic and fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you know of the existence of either the Patriotic League or the Green Berets prior to the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a notorious fact, especially the Patriotic League, which was very strong in Tuzla. But this was a secret organisation whereas the Green Berets were a semi-secret organisation. I can't say that I saw them anywhere lined up but it was well known to everybody that the Green Berets existed. Later on, the Patriotic League committed a massacre against a column of the JNA that was withdrawing from Tuzla towards Serbia according to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Maricic, can you be more specific? Perhaps we should break the two organisations down. So far as the Patriotic League is concerned, I repeat, this is your knowledge prior to the outbreak of the war, where did it come from, and what did you understand about that organisation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I had information that the Patriotic League is a Muslim organisation. And that it was some sort of a secret armed formation, organisation, which in my view was under the control and command of the SDA. And the Green Berets, bearing in mind that the word "green" is in their name, the green being a symbol of Muslims, was also an organisation under the control of the Muslims or to the SDA, and both these organisations were semi-military and, needless to say, secret organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why were you of the view that the Patriotic League was under the control and command of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: This is the information I received and there was no reason for me not to believe it because I was already familiar with the events in Brcko and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was information that came from all sides and it was no longer a big unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you be more specific as to the source of the information?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to specify something, please. Before the outbreak of the war, in those days that preceded the first war operations, did you meet any Green Berets? In other words, did you realise that there were Muslim fighters whom you could see in the street? Or all this -- or was all of this kept secret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see them, and it was kept a secret. Only after the war have we learned that they were established and we now know where they were trained, in what camps, where their checkpoints were, where their instructors were, and we now know that their instructors had come from Arabic countries and that these people trained them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one follow-up question as well. You told us that the military intelligence service was aware of all that, talking about weapons smuggled from Croatia. What military intelligence service you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there was a single military intelligence service within the JNA and I believe that it had eyes and ears everywhere. It was a very organised organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, so it is military intelligence within the JNA. How did they report? How did you get to know about this knowledge within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that. But there were rumours and every now and then a secret leaked. Those officers, intelligence officers, had wives, had neighbours, so sometime secrets would leak and reach us common people, and I was a curious person and I wanted to know, and that's how I learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to blame wives and neighbours only for leaking, Mr. Maricic, is -- but thank you for your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to ask you about whether you had any knowledge of the arming of Croats. Again, before the war, please.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that the chief of police, although Croats were less numerous than Muslims, they had a prominent role, and whatever they did, they could cover it up because the chief of police belonged to them. We received information that young lads were crossing the Sava from Croatia and elsewhere, and that they carried in their bags uniforms for both Muslim and Croat military units. This was no longer a secret. And also there were rumours that were confirmed after the war, they transported weapons for both Muslims and Croats across the Sava. These weapons were under the control of Croats because it came from Croatia. There is a notorious affair, Spegelj, and Croatia had influence on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is no wonder that Croat-Muslim brigade which was billeted in Brcko, was the -- called the HVO Brigade, although two-thirds of its strength were Muslims. There was no obstacle to the transport of weapons from Croatia into Brcko. This was a well-known fact which was -- was kept a secret but now this secret has been confirmed after the war. I don't have any more details, nothing more precise to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next topic I would like to turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it may be clear to you that what was known already, whether through wives or neighbours, and what has been confirmed after the war, and what they could have done in covering up, et cetera, et cetera. He does not give a lot of, as we say in our language, hands and feet, to the testimony. So I take it that you're aware that without further exploring these matters, that it's -- I'm note saying it's of no assistance but at least this is information which is relatively vague and at least not as precise in the statement which would as easily allow us to find corroboration in details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could be allowed to comment on the evidence, Your Honour, the witness is being what the Court may think is disarmingly frank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he's not frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: His source of information, his lack of information, and how he learned a lot of this subsequently, and therefore from the Defence point of view, how productive it will be in trying to break this down, I don't know, and I'm more inclined to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed. Mr. Maricic would like to say something, I think. Mr. Maricic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say -- I see that people are saying what I'm saying is imprecise, and it is. But I remember a case when an ambulance driver in January 1992, a Serb, told me that Muslims and Croats from the hospital, and the hospital had some weapons for defence, including machine-guns, any way he told me that Muslims and Croats stole all those weapons that only seven or eight pistols remained. Somebody was caught selling those pistols later. But I remember this man, and he's still alive. I remember now that he told me that Muslims and Croats had stolen the weapons for the security of the hospital. And since Croats and Muslims were in leading positions in Brcko, all the archives were taken by them and given to the Muslim or Croat side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Josse? Do you remember the name of the driver of this ambulance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Dusan Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether he's still alive or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He is a taxi driver in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm still trying to sort out the logistical matter that Your Honour had referred to at the beginning of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next topic I would like to ask you about, again in the pre-war period, is the SDS. It's right, and perhaps we didn't say this because I didn't ask you earlier, that you were on the main board of the SDS in the first year of its existence, 1990 to 1991?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1991, do you recall any visits to Brcko from prominent members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I can't remember all those details now. I suppose somebody came. A year couldn't have passed without anybody coming, but I can't give you a name. You probably are not interested in small fry, and as for bigger names I can't remember them. I suppose they did come, though. One year is a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you specifically, then, about a meeting of an organisation called Prosveta, in 1991. I may have completely mispronounced that. It's P-r-o-s-v-e-t-a.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood what you mean. This founding meeting or not really founding assembly but restoration assembly, because Prosveta did not exist among the Serb people after the Second World War, it was forbidden, so after the first free elections the Serbian people restored this cultural and enlightening organisation, Prosveta, including for the town of Brcko. However, I did not attend that assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea, from second hand sources, therefore, whether either Mr. Krajisnik or Dr. Karadzic attended that assembly, as you described it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Since both Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were already very famous people, I would have remembered if one of them had attended. Brcko is not such a big town that I could have missed it. I would have certainly been aware if one of them had come to that assembly. I heard later that some other people attended, famous writers, poets, but that's completely different. None of the two were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting Mr. Krajisnik at all prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: No. No. I met up with Mr. Krajisnik for the first time very late, by force of circumstance. I didn't see him at meetings of the executive council. He kept a low profile and I also kept to the backbenches. But I saw him on television, when he was speaker of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I watched him on TV at assembly meetings. Those were hard times and I saw that he led the assembly very successfully, and managed to deal with many tricky situations. That's when I first saw Mr. Krajisnik, that is, on the television. And it was only a long time later, in 1994, that I met him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you referred in your last answer to the executive council, you were referring, I presume, to the main board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I meant to say the main board of the party. I was a member of the main board of the SDS as it was founded, and I said he kept a low profile on the main board. I didn't ever see him asked to speak at sessions of the main board while I was a member. I was surprised to find out that he had been a member of the main board, ever since it was founded, because I never saw him in those meetings or maybe I didn't notice him. Maybe he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, to have a look at this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm about to hand out, I think is reflected in P21. P21 is quite heavily marked. I have taken this map from an exhibit which I think wasn't used, a potential Prosecution exhibit much earlier in the case. Literally at its start, in fact. I received it on a CD in colour. Unfortunately I've been unable to reproduce that but I think this will do. I have a lighter copy for the ELMO so perhaps this one could be put on the ELMO and plenty of other copies for everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want the witness to mark that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then let's have a look at it and then let's proceed. Mr. Josse, if any marking will be needed, black is the colour for the Defence. Blue is the colour for the Prosecution. And I think red is the colour for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Black is going to be not very satisfactory on this map but let's see how we get on. I don't want to upset a well-tried and-trusted system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This, Mr. Maricic, is Brcko, and we can see two bridges, one on the right of the map is clearly a railway bridge, and the one in the middle of the map is a road bridge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is not in dispute that on the 30th of April, there were explosions at and around those bridges, is it? You accept that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All I want to ask you about is whether there were any explosions at or around either of those bridges prior to the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Croats from the Croatian side, because those bridges lead to Croatia, and there was already fighting going on around Vukovar. It could have been maybe a month into the war in Brcko. So the Croats had laid mines and explosives to both those bridges from their side. The railway bridge was completely disabled for railway traffic. And this other bridge for passenger cars and pedestrians was also damaged, bombed from the Croatian side, but the Croats then put up planks so that pedestrians could still get across. Of course, that caused even greater concern among Serbs in Brcko because they felt they were being surrounded, encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For clarification, you have just used the expression, "A month into the war in Brcko." When do you say, bearing in mind that expression, that the war in Brcko started?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
