utterances.text: Well, I think there is no dispute about that. The war started in Brcko on the 1st of May, or maybe the evening of the -- 2nd May, the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I may comment, I think there is no dispute about that. What I want to ask you about is -- what I have been asking you about, perhaps I should say, is the attacks on these bridges. The attack that you say was carried out by Croatians, when did that occur in relation to the 1st of May? Before? After? How long? That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I think a month before the 1st of May, roughly speaking. I think that happened rather a long time, let's say a month, before the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the answer you've just given a moment or two ago clarifies the damage that you say was carried out in the course of that attack. Why did you understand -- let me rephrase that. What was the perception among Serbs at the time as to the reason the Croats had attempted to disable both these bridges?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Already then, a month before the war started, Serbs were seized by panic. Every new incident increased their fear. It wasn't understood why the Croats destroyed those bridges but it certainly had a negative impact on the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was there any shooting in Brcko prior to the second attack on the bridges on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: There was no shooting in Brcko before the war began, except that when the war was going on in Croatia, Brcko is very close by, and people who fought around Vukovar would come to Brcko. We called them ZNGs, Home Guards Corps, members. They would come to Brcko and create incidents in the bars and pubs of Brcko, and one person in the uniform of the Home Guards Corps of Croatia lost his life at the entrance to the casino.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date but I passed by with my son and I saw that man outside the casino. He had gotten killed the previous night, and his body lay there for almost one whole day. The tensions were already high. Muslims and Croats were passing by. Serbs by that time didn't dare be around very much. That boy was a native of Drenovac, a village from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When the -- let me start again. When do you say the second attack on the bridges occurred? Can you give us a precise date?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: The second attack on the bridges, from the Brcko side, was on the 30th of April, I believe. I believe that's the last month -- that's the last day before the 1st of May. I heard a terrible explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where were you when you heard a terrible explosion?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I went to a village named Stanovi, about five or six kilometres east of Brcko to see a friend, and in view of the tensions I decided to stay the night. And around 5.00 in the morning, I heard terrible explosions. If they were heard five or six kilometres away, I can imagine how horribly they resounded in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you have a look at the map of Brcko and perhaps you could show the Chamber - it will need to be put back on the ELMO - where it was you were spending the night when you heard these terrible explosions?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Well, if this is the centre of the town, there are no villages shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Wrong map. That's why. It's the wrong map. Sorry, I didn't make that clear enough. I'm grateful to Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I can't find my way around this map. Well, I was here somewhere. I see Brezik village and Stanovi is not far away. Those are neighbouring village. I can't see Stanovi itself but they must be around here since Brezik is here. Right, here they are. Stanovi village, where I spent that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you mark that with a black pen, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Shall I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's you that needs to mark it, Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we will give it some other form of identification, if the map needs to be marked in some other way. I suspect it will, in fact, in due course. Did you have any idea that this attack on the bridges was going to take place?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely no clue. I think only the perpetrators could have known. And even though I was a rather well informed and moved around all sorts of circles, I had no clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did you return to Brcko after the explosions?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I think around 9 or 10.00 the next day, I drove back in my own car, and I went to see what happened to the bridges, out of curiosity. I didn't go to see the railway bridge because it was too far away. The other, the passenger bridge, was in the centre. It was surrounded by the police so I couldn't get close. But I saw from a distance of about 40 metres that the bridge was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was it either obvious or were there any rumours, information, at that point, as to who had done this and why they had done it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: It is not obvious, not even today. We Serbs were thinking that maybe some divers had come from Croatia on a boat and did it. I can't tell you even now with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You had mentioned that after the first attack, the road bridge was incapable of carrying vehicular traffic but was still able to take pedestrians. What was the effect on the bridge of the second attack?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Communications were absolutely broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did matters progress in the town at that point?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Panic in town was complete. Everybody was running to their own side. Large numbers of Muslims were running southeast, Croats together with them, or perhaps more to the south, and Serbs were running east towards Bijeljina because the psychosis of war had already been complete and that was the last drop to set off the panic and make people run. A lot of people escaped then and only the more courageous, able-bodied men remained, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, each in their own zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know how the fighting actually began in the town?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was again visiting with this friend in Stanovi village and I just heard shooting in the night coming from Grcica, a suburb populated mostly by Serbs. There, in the part of the suburb bordering on Muslims and Croat areas, Muslims and Croats had put up their barricades, I don't know if there were any Serb barricades but I know that from what I heard, the Muslims and Croats started shooting from those barricades at Serbs, and that's what started the war in Brcko, from what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From whom did you hear that that is how the war started in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: As I said, complete panic reigned and the fever of war had overtaken everybody. Only some able-bodied men were there and it didn't seem a strange thing to happen under the circumstances. There were all sorts of rumours. Nobody came to inform me in particular. It was just common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you do when you learned that the shooting had started?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I just stayed where I was because I had lived in Brka for a while. I wasn't really mobilised into this Territorial Defence so that they could assign me somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At what point did you move back into the centre of Brcko, to your home?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I didn't go downtown to my house. While I was still at Stanovi village, a group of soldiers found me there. They told me they were Mauzer's men and they were collecting whoever they found outside the town, and they took me to a front line on the bank of the Brka river. I got a weapon and I became a soldier of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Using either map, show us where Mauzer's men took you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is the Brka river, and I was taken somewhere around here, across the Brka river, because Muslims had established a Defence line somewhere here, and on this side here, there were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Please mark that with a black pen.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. I would just like to say that the war operations had already started, and that the line was somewhere around here. A whole day and night before I was taken to the line, there were already combat activities going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you remember the day you arrived at the line? The date, rather than the day, the date.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was on the 2nd of May, or maybe on the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, for the position of the transcript, I think we should ask the witness to add an M to the vertical line close to the Sava River, close to the most northerly bridge on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite understand where I have to put this M.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next to the marking you just made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the point that you went to this front line and you begun combat activities, are you able to help the Chamber as to the degree to which the JNA had become involved in the dispute?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I've said that the JNA in Brcko was reduced to some 20 officers and non-commissioned officers. The recruits that already abandoned the JNA. I never saw them. On the line where I was taken there was the Territorial Defence consisting of the Serbian people of Brcko and I didn't see a single JNA officer there at all. Throughout all that time that I spent on that front line, I didn't see a single JNA officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it might help if next you described how long you spent at that position over the next two weeks or so. You've already told the Chamber and, as I say we'll deal with this in more detail in due course, that you were badly wounded on the 16th of May. So between the 3rd of May and the 16th of May, how much time did you spend in the position that you have marked M on the map?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I spent maybe a day and a half in this position. The line moved forward and, having been recruited, I had to move with the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened after the day and a half?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: The front line was moved westwards along the Sava River, and together with the rest of the Serbian army, I had to move as well. I was not a weakling, I was a good fighter, and we moved forward. I suppose you're going to ask me some more questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Maricic, for my part, I'm less concerned with operational details. Others may be interested in that. I'm more concerned as to whether you physically remained at the front or whether you were able to go to the town centre and see what was happening, or whether you went to your home, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: Throughout all that time, I was on the front line. I did have an opportunity, and not only I, since the front line was very stable. So every soldier could be given an hour or so to go home. Not always but sometimes you could have that. And since I was not a member of the corps strength, I had some privileges and although I was in a position to go, I didn't go that often. I was not recruited with the first wave but with the second wave. So I did have an opportunity to go home, but I think I went only once or twice. Once I went to have a bath and I don't know whether I went a second time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you mark your home on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I can give you just an approximation. This map is not very precise. I can give you a rough idea, if you want me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That will be fine, as far as I'm concerned, Mr. Maricic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you add an H to that as for your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On the occasions that you were able to leave the line and return to your home, I want to ask you about your awareness of various events. For the purpose of this question, I'm including the whole period from the start of the war to the point that you were invalided out of it. Paramilitary units, were you aware of their presence in Brcko at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: All the strings of the military shoes in Brcko were pulled by the leftists, i.e. people who were members of the League of Communists and who were in good relations with the JNA. I was on the exactly opposite side so that many events escaped me. They were hidden from me. And as for the paramilitary units and their arrival, I know very little about that because of my very different political affiliation and those things were kept secret from me. That is my explanation why I don't know how they came. I only know that I saw them in town, in small numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could deal with this a slightly different way. You have mentioned that you were taken to the front line by Mauzer's men. Which army, if any, did you regard yourself a member of at that point?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: At the time I was taken there, this was not a classical military. All the able-bodied Serbian people had been gathered, they were given weapons, organised into some sort of units, to defend themselves. The organisation was very poor and it would be very far-fetched to call all that an army. This is my view of the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Doesn't -- that's useful information, as far as the Defence are concerned, Mr. Maricic, but it doesn't actually answer the question. As far as you were concerned, were you the member of an army, and if so, at that time, under what title did it go?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: It didn't have a name. I can say that I was a member of the army of the Serbian people but that army did not have a name. There is no single document in which it is referred to as the Serbian army. Maybe the closest description would be the people's Territorial Defence. There was no other official name. And I belonged to those formations of the Serbian people that defended the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just to clarify that, did your battalion or brigade have any epithet attached or given to it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: No. When combat operations started, I remember that there were only three squads in Brcko and they had not even been united into a battalion. And when I was taken there, I was taken to the so-called third squad. There were only three squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So how had it got -- was it known as the 3rd squad?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I believe so. It was known as a third squad or company. There were the 1st Company, the 2nd Company and the 3rd Company. I don't know whether the third company was in the middle of the front line but this is where I was taken. I was given a rifle and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The 3rd Company of what, please?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MARICIC
utterances.text: I can't answer because I don't know. I know that there were the 1st, the 2nd and the 3rd companies, but I don't know that they were segments of a battalion or any other higher-ranking unit. If you want me to talk about the JNA, I can say that there was no JNA to speak of. There were just some 20 officers and a -- non-commissioned officers who left on the 19th of May, save for those who hailed from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on and deal with some specific questions in relation to paramilitaries. I'm happy to do that now or later. I'm in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better to have a break first. We'll have a break until 10 minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before we continue with the examination of Mr. Maricic, I'd like to deliver a few -- make a few statements. I will start with a request for re-translation of Exhibit P824, and the submission of the Official Gazette of the Serb assembly 11, 92. There are two matters the Chamber would like to address regarding Exhibit P824, tab 1. This is a decision on, and I quote, "Determination of acquired rights based on tenancy rights and labour relations" taken by the Serb assembly of Hadzici municipality. The Chamber has reasons to believe that the translation of Article 1 of the decision might be imprecise. Therefore, the Chamber requests the Prosecution to resubmit the whole decision to CLSS and to provide the Chamber with a new translation. Furthermore, the preamble of the decision refers to the Official Gazette number 11 of 1992 and the Chamber requests the Prosecution to inquire whether the issue of the Official Gazette is available and to submit it to the Chamber by the 30th of March. This concludes this request. Then I'd like to make a statement on the admission of exhibits and translations. The first matter the Chamber would like to address is the fact that several exhibits still require either translation or, in the case of audio exhibits, accompanying CDs. In addition to those previously addressed by the Chamber, the Chamber awaits translation of items P1077, P1079, P1081, P1082, P1084, P1090, and the written text of P1092. We also await CDs of items P1083 and P1088, up to and including P1091. Additionally the Prosecution tendered item P1092, and here I refer to transcript pages 21119 to 21121, as both a written press report and a video segment. The Chamber asks the Prosecution to submit the video footage as P1092A, the English transcript of the video as P1092A.1 and the B/C/S transcript of the video as P1092A.2. The Defence tendered items D144, an extract from a newspaper, and D145, consisting of four pages of an interview with Jovo Radojko in English, specifically pages 27, 28, 29, and 30. The Chamber asks the Defence to provide the Registry with the translations of these documents. The Chamber asks the parties to submit to the Registrar all of the above-mentioned items by the 5th of April 2006. The second matter the Chamber would like to address relates to two items introduced during the testimony of Witness Savkic. With respect to P1065, a daily report dated the 7th of June 1992, and P1066, an order dated the 7th of June 1992, the Chamber recalls that they have been subject to substantial disagreement between the parties. I specifically refer to transcript pages 20.679 to 20.701, 20.703 to 20.704, 20.813 to 20.815, 20.825 to 20.827, 20.975, 20.978 to 20.984, as well as the submissions of the parties last Friday the 17th of March 2006. The Defence has argued that the witness had no knowledge of the contents or provenance of these two documents and that the witness stated or implied that they were forgeries. The Prosecution submitted that these items were proper impeachment documents. The party introducing evidence need not prove that a document is not a forgery in order to -- for it to be admitted into evidence. Unless it is conclusively shown in court that a document is falsified, its reliability may depend on the totality of the evidence and may only be capable of definitive determination at a later stage of the proceedings. Reliability should be left for assessment when considering the weight a piece of evidence will be given. When a witness and a document appear to contradict each other, it may be appropriate to admit both pieces of evidence into the trial record. This may be the only way for the Chamber to be able at a later stage to assess the reliability of both the witness and the document. The Chamber therefore admits both P1065 and P1066 into evidence. The third matter the Chamber would like to address is the admission of item P1104. The Chamber has considered the arguments of the parties, especially at transcript pages 21.497 to 21.498. This is a news agency report that was presented to the witness. The Chamber notes that many similar documents have been admitted during these proceedings. D62 is an example of a news agency report admitted into evidence at a request of the Accused even though the witness confronted with it clearly stated that he did not have any access to the television or newspapers during the relevant period. Once again, the Chamber considers the matter raised by the Defence to be properly dealt with when considering the weight of this document and not at the admission stage. Therefore, the Chamber admits the document into evidence. The fourth and final matter the Chamber would like to attend to is the admission of Exhibits tendered by both parties. The following exhibits were submitted during the testimony of previous witnesses and await entry into evidence: For the Prosecution, P1055 to P1057, P1059, P1060, P1074 to P1076, P1078, P1080, and P1085 to P1087, P1097 to P1103, and P1105 to P1108. For the Defence, D142 and D143. The Chamber requests the parties to submit any objections to these exhibits right away. I do understand that the parties have been informed by the staff of Chambers that this issue would be raised. So therefore if there are any objections the Chamber would like to hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What, now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My papers are in the Defence room in relation to Poplasen. That wasn't made sufficiently clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's then say that latest by tomorrow, any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've done the work so far as Mr. Poplasen is concerned. I simply need to physically bring my notes into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you'll get time for that and next time you appear in court we'll hear any objections. Mr. Harmon any objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then with a final decision, we will await, Mr. Josse, until we have heard from you. I would like to express my admiration at this moment for the transcribers who so successfully put into the transcript all those numbers read out by me. I admire the job they are doing where we very often address the translators -- the interpreters and the technicians, I would take this opportunity to express the -- our appreciation for the excellent work done by the transcribers as well. Then, Mr. Josse, then we could continue, I take it, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm ready, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher. I also take the opportunity, Mr. Josse, I am aware that you're concerned about tomorrow's session. We are still looking whether an alternative would be possible, and I hope to receive additional information still during this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are trying as best we can to make any contingency plans, if the Chamber is aware of the results at the time of rising I would be grateful because it involves matters to do with the UNDU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Chamber will try and see whether it would be possible to sit tomorrow in the afternoon, but we are then certain the only possibility is to do that after the Stakic judgement has been delivered. And then, of course, we would need sometime for the change of the tapes so we would lose, most likely, approximately two hours of the afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would move -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I thought we were going to sit all tomorrow afternoon under the plan that Your Honour was mooting originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm making a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not originally, the plan Your Honour was mooting after the last break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about moving from morning to the afternoon. And, yes, that caused you the problem so, yes, but Stakic is in the morning, I think it is planned in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is a -- they moved the delivery of the Stakic judgement from morning to afternoon. That caused some confusion. So that is not a solution at this moment. Let's first start with the witness. We'll deal with the matter at the very end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic, I said at the commencement of the last break that I was at this juncture going to ask you some more questions about your knowledge of paramilitary activity in Brcko in the two weeks or so after the war broke out and before you were wounded. Rather than ask you generally, let me ask you about your state of knowledge very specific groups. Firstly, the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about White Eagles. I never heard or saw those people in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about forces under the command of Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they were White Eagles. That was something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry. I'm not suggesting that Captain Dragan had anything to do with the White Eagles. You've given your answer about the White Eagles. I'm now asking you about Captain Dragan and his men.

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard sometime at the beginning of the war, and I even ran into three or four young men who I was told were under Captain Dragan but I only ran into, like, three or four of them, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any other information, knowledge, about Captain Dragan's forces?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While I was wounded, I was in hospital in Belgrade, and once captain Dragan came to visit wounded men, including me. That's the only time I saw him. I didn't see any other fighting men around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about Arkan and his forces?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen Arkan in person. I don't think he ever came to Brcko. As for Arkan's men, I believe there were fewer of them than Captain Dragan's men, but they were strong, in terms of influence, and their influence far exceeded their numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did their influence manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they all had some sort of pseudonyms. They had ranks like colonels, Lieutenant colonels, all of them seemed to have some sort of high rank. They were rather arrogant and they simply imposed themselves and issued commands. I'm talking about the period after the war just began.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move on to Mauzer and his forces. What can you tell the Chamber about him and his men?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mauzer brought this Territorial Defence to Brcko, and those units he brought numbered several hundred. Within them was a smaller unit called Mauzer's guard. At that time, this Mauzer person made the weather and he had no commander above him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The expression "made the weather" is not one that I understand. Could you explain what that means, please?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Maricic. You're the man in the hot spot at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago that Mauzer "made the weather" and had no commander above him. I didn't understand what you meant by the expression "made the weather." Can you explain that phraseology?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mauzer was a man who is full of himself. He commanded his own men but also everybody else. He simply imposed himself as the commander. Nobody dared oppose him. The only thing I noticed is that he sort of appreciated and respected those Red Berets of Captain Dragan. As for the locals, he didn't care for them much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you refer to locals, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the troops or rather the armed men among whom I was, those two or three companies, and the company commanders. To them, Mauzer was the highest authority. Not in formal terms but it's simply that he imposed himself on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So to be clear by locals you mean local Serbs, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Armed local Serbs and civilians as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the first two weeks of the war, who was commanding the local Serb war effort, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some men like company commanders, I can't remember their names. One was Boro Borislav, he was commanding the unit to which I belonged. But I can't remember the others. All of them were absolutely obedient to Mauzer. Mauzer decided on the deployment of those forces on the front line and decided all such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you see Mauzer in the two-week period that we are --

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the part of the front line that I described earlier and that I marked on the map, when a man came who said he was Mauzer's deputy, and said that my unit, my part of the troops, should move towards the hospital. Then some sort of confusion occurred. That man left. Mauzer himself arrived, gathered as many people as he wished, and took them towards the hospital. That's one occasion when I saw him and I saw him two or three times after that, and I saw him again after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to go back, if I may, to the JNA. Who was the JNA commander, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the commander in Brcko was Pavle Milenkovic. He was commander of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how was he involved in the fighting, if at all?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him. He was in the barracks. What he did and how, I don't know. It's certain that he was not an unimportant person but Mauzer was far more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the name Captain Petrovic mean anything in relation to that period?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew captain Petrovic and I met him once or twice in town before the war. He was chief of security at the barracks in Brcko, chief of military security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall him being on the television at the start of the war with a local Muslim leader?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rumour had it that he appeared on television together with Mustafa Ramic, but I didn't see that myself. I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with Mustafa Ramic in the first two weeks of the war?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of my statements, I said that I had gone out to town to take a shower, and just out of curiosity, I toured the town to see what things were like and I was passing by the barracks. There was one room in the barracks just next to the street, and I heard a man shouting from that room, "Come, Bosko, come. And report." I said, "Report to who?" And the man said, "Mustafa Ramic is calling you." I noticed that it was a military person and I didn't want to report but eventually I did come to Mustafa Ramic. When the combat began in Brcko, he was their chief military commander under the nickname Babo. So they put me on and he asked me, "Can I do something to stop the war?" And I said spontaneously, "Look, we need -- we need to do something. Your people will get killed but so will ours." And Mustafa Ramic said, "Go and talk it through with your people. I'll talk it through with mine and let's talk again in half an hour." But he didn't call back and later I went back to my unit. That's all I have to say about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the fortnight period that you are presently describing, what was your understanding as to what was happening to Muslims who were living in Serb-held parts of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a long story. As the front line moved, one number of Muslims got captured. From what I know, but I only heard about it, there were some people, Serbs, from the police, who were interrogated. Anyone who was established to have taken part in the fighting was singled out, put on one side, and all the others were released. That's what I know about captives and the treatment of captives. When I went from the front line to town, I noticed a few dead bodies along the road. I even recognised one or two. They were local Muslims, people I used to know, and it was a harrowing experience. If I had to go -- if I had somewhere to go, I would have deserted the front line then. But after that, I gave it some thought. I realised it was wartime, and war does not spare anyone, innocent or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, firstly at the map of Brcko town that you have marked. Using the pointer, perhaps you can describe how the front line moved. Describe is the wrong word. Demonstrate, please.

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only guess. I was not involved in any organisational work or map drawing but I can tell you how the front line moved in the area where I was. I marked already the spot where I found myself when I first came to the front line. This is the line held by Muslims and Croats in the place where I was. The front line moved along the Sava River and there is a road going towards Banja Luka here. Around here should be the hospital. And the front line went there. All along the edges of the town. When the town was behind, the front line curved and continued over here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, if you would, Mr. Maricic, at the other map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I leave it to you to make it clear for anyone who will look at the transcript at a later stage to understand what the witness just pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I'm going to do, Your Honour, is give him perhaps another one of these maps of the Brcko municipality and ask him to mark it overnight. That might be a time-consuming way of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until now, of course, we are dealing only with the city, the town, rather than what the witness just said was about how the front line moved in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The problem, of course, was he went well outside through no fault of his own the bounds of the map. He was pointing to the area that borders the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at the same time, there is some ambiguity into what he actually knows, what he has seen, at least it -- he started his answer by saying, "Well, I can only guess," which, of course, is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not encouraging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, those are your words but I would not contradict them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Maricic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I leave it to you what request we will put to the witness to do overnight with the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Looking at the larger map the front line was somewhere near Ivici is that right?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivik. That's where the front line was when I was wounded at Ivik -- Ivici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it is Ivici on the map, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Bosko Maricic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it's Ivici. Ivici with a diacritic on the C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the map it appears northwestern part is the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a moment I will cherish where I more or less pronounced it right the first time. Would you be able to, using this map of the municipality, draw a line as to where you understood the front line to be at the point that you were invalided out of the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, before the witness answers the question, how important, relevant, is it to know where it is? Are you going to give this any follow-up or would it be enough to say, well, it moved to the west or it moved to the east?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would undoubtedly be enough. I was only asking him to mark it as a result of Your Honour's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I said, as a matter of fact, what he explained to us before, that it's not easy to follow that on the transcript without any marking but we could ask the witness, this front line, Mr. Maricic, which as you indicated earlier, went somewhere through town in the beginning, did this move to the west or to the east or did it not move at all? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It moved. It shifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It shifted. What direction, west, east?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] West and then also to southwest, and later south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And finally, was the front line still within town or moved in such a way that front line left the town, so to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The front line remained within the town all the way until end 1994. It remained within the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I see, for example, on the map, Kalanac [phoen], Ivici. Was it finally in that area that the front line was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse? It seems that the front line moved to the most western part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm content with that, if Your Honour is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Yes, Mr. Maricic, you would like to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add that to the west side, there was also the main road to Banja Luka, and this part of the front line that went along that road practically connected with the front line in Posavina, so the corridor towards Banja Luka was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps finally on this, the -- no. I'll deal with that tomorrow, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock and since I said that we would leave the -- tomorrow's session to the end of today, perhaps this would be a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would be convenient, Your Honour. Perhaps these two maps should be numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because they have not yet received a number. Let's first start with the black and white map of the town marked by the witness. That would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D150, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D150. Then you say the other map. The other map was not marked by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be -- yes, Mr. Registrar that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D151, Your Honours, with the ERN number 03646512.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the coloured map was not marked by the witness, was it? I see -- I've got it in front of me, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was. He circled where he spent the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Stanovi. I fully agree with you. It's Stanovi which is marked, yes. I had forgotten that. That would then be D151. Yes. Then, Mr. Maricic, we have a practical problem on our hearing for tomorrow. We are scheduled to sit in the morning. Then we received a request to move to the afternoon. We have not finally decided yet what to do because there were some other problems involved as well. So therefore, we will adjourn until tomorrow, but unfortunately I can't tell you yet whether we'll sit in the morning or in the afternoon. You'll be informed about that by the victims and witnesses section and I apologise for the inconvenience it may cause but we hope to inform you as soon as possible. Then could you please follow Madam Usher and -- but not -- but not -- one second. But not until I have instructed you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have already given and you're still about to give. So you should not speak with anyone about it. Then please follow Madam Usher and we would like to see you back tomorrow, whether morning or afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, first of all, how much time you would still need for your examination-in-chief with this witness, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Another session, frankly, I would have thought maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another session maximum. Mr. Harmon, any idea already on time your cross-examination will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour. I can't assist you. At least a session, possibly more. But it depends on my analysis of his evidence this evening and tomorrow's evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the limits the Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of course, being very careful with the 60 per cent rule, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, now is as good a time to -- not to grapple with this but to alert the Chamber to the fact, if the Chamber has looked closely at our most recent filings we are in real difficulty as to evidence for Friday, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To what extent that affects the thinking for tomorrow, I don't know, probably not at all, but I do mention that in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's in your fourth request, you would say. Well, let's say today it's Tuesday. We would certainly not start the next witness tomorrow because he will arrive only in the afternoon from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct. There was no possibility of starting him tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That means that we, at earliest if you were in a position to properly prepare, that you could perhaps start on Thursday, depending on how matters go tomorrow. What, then, would be your problem for Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He may have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He may have finished within one day?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Though I personally have not spent a great deal of time considering his evidence, we anticipate as a general proposition him being shorter than some of the witnesses -- well, the last few witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the time estimate is including cross, isn't it, on your -- the fourth of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say that -- and the witness who is now scheduled for Monday would not arrive until?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Friday at the earliest, and he remains unwell, frankly. We are in not just daily I think twice daily contact with him, and the prognosis literally vacillates from morning to evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you expect the witness to come after Mr. Maricic will most likely not take more than one day in total?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He may not. That's the best I can say. I'm perhaps being unduly pessimistic here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take that into consideration when we will give a decision. We'll let you know as soon as possible because I do understand your problems. I hope you understand that other Chambers have problems as well and that we are only trying to accommodate everyone as good as possible but sometimes it's not possible to make everyone happy. So whether it would be you, whether it would be the Defence or the other Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour I've spoken to Mr. Stewart and he says we will cope as best we can with, of course, whatever order the court makes in this regard. I've simply made some observations about the practical difficulties involved. There is nothing more I can usefully add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will carefully consider them and we will inform the parties on shortest notice whether we'll sit in the morning or the afternoon. Then we will adjourn until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
